emt-obgyn-peds-l01.q: A 30-week pregnant patient is trapped in a car. Her respiratory rate is 28 and her pulse oximeter reads 91%. Why does her oxygen level fall so fast?
choices: The uterus pushes the diaphragm up, so her oxygen reserve is small
Pregnancy lowers the amount of hemoglobin available to carry oxygen
The extra blood volume dilutes the oxygen in each breath
Pregnancy hormones slow the rate the lungs absorb oxygen
emt-obgyn-peds-l01.why: The enlarged uterus shoves the diaphragm upward, shrinking the reserve volume in the lungs, so saturation drops within seconds of any interruption. Oxygen-carrying capacity is actually higher in pregnancy, not lower.

emt-obgyn-peds-l01.q: You must perform CPR on a 34-week pregnant patient lying flat on a hard surface. What do you do about the uterus?
choices: Tilt the whole patient 30 degrees left and compress at an angle
Have a rescuer push the uterus up and toward her left while she stays flat
Place a wedge under her left hip so she rolls right
Leave her flat; positioning does not matter once she is in arrest
emt-obgyn-peds-l01.why: Compressions need a flat, hard surface, so the answer is manual uterine displacement: a gloved rescuer pushes the uterus up and to the patient's left to free the vena cava. Tilting degrades compression quality, and a right-side wedge makes the compression worse.

emt-obgyn-peds-l02.q: A 29-week pregnant patient has a BP of 158/98, a severe headache and swollen hands. Her partner hands you her aspirin bottle and asks if she should take one. What is the correct answer?
choices: Give one 325 mg aspirin to lower the pressure
Give 81 mg of aspirin because it protects the placenta
No aspirin; position her left lateral, keep stimulation low and transport to an obstetric hospital
No aspirin, but give nitroglycerin if her systolic is above 150
emt-obgyn-peds-l02.why: Preeclampsia is a whole-body vessel problem treated with magnesium and delivery, neither of which an EMT carries. Aspirin and nitroglycerin are cardiac answers and do nothing here; the field treatment is position, quiet and speed.

emt-obgyn-peds-l02.q: A 26-year-old with lower abdominal pain insists she cannot be pregnant because she uses an IUD. She is pale, HR 124, BP 92/58, with almost no vaginal bleeding. What should you assume?
choices: Ovarian cyst, since an IUD makes pregnancy essentially impossible
Ruptured ectopic pregnancy bleeding into the abdomen
Kidney stone, which explains the pain and pallor
Appendicitis, which is more common at her age
emt-obgyn-peds-l02.why: No contraception is perfect, and shock out of proportion to visible bleeding in a woman of childbearing age is a ruptured ectopic until proven otherwise. A stone or appendicitis does not produce this degree of hypoperfusion this fast.

emt-obgyn-peds-l03.q: A patient having her first baby has contractions 7 minutes apart lasting 40 seconds and there is no crowning. The hospital is 15 minutes away. What is correct?
choices: Deliver on scene, since first labors go fastest
Have her push with each contraction to speed things up
Transport in the left lateral position and reassess for crowning
Perform a vaginal exam to measure how dilated she is
emt-obgyn-peds-l03.why: Contractions this far apart with no crowning mean there is time to move, and a first labor is typically the slowest. EMTs never perform vaginal exams, and coaching pushing before the cervix is ready accomplishes nothing.

emt-obgyn-peds-l03.q: The head has delivered and the baby's face is covered by the amniotic sac membrane. What do you do?
choices: Tear or slip the membrane off the face immediately so the baby can breathe
Leave it alone; it will rupture as the shoulders deliver
Suction through the membrane with the bulb syringe
Clamp and cut the cord first, then remove the membrane
emt-obgyn-peds-l03.why: An intact sac over the face blocks the first breath, so tear it and wipe it clear at once. Waiting or suctioning through it wastes the seconds the baby needs, and the cord is not the problem.

emt-obgyn-peds-l04.q: During a shoulder dystocia your partner reaches for the top of the uterus to push down. Why must you stop him?
choices: Fundal pressure drives the stuck shoulder harder into the pubic bone
Fundal pressure causes the placenta to deliver too early
Fundal pressure ruptures the amniotic sac
Fundal pressure has no effect, so it only wastes time
emt-obgyn-peds-l04.why: Pressure on the fundus pushes the baby straight down onto the bone the shoulder is already hung up on, wedging it tighter and risking injury. The correct pressure is suprapubic, just above the pubic bone, aimed at rotating the shoulder free.

emt-obgyn-peds-l04.q: You deliver twins in the ambulance. What must you do before the second baby arrives?
choices: Deliver the first placenta completely
Clamp and cut the first baby's cord
Wait at least 10 minutes before allowing the second to deliver
Massage the fundus firmly until the uterus is hard
emt-obgyn-peds-l04.why: The first cord must be clamped before the second twin delivers, because the twins may share placental circulation and the second delivery can bleed the first baby through an open cord. The placenta or placentas come after both babies, and firm fundal massage before the second twin is out is wrong.

emt-obgyn-peds-l05.q: You listen to a newborn's chest for 6 seconds and count 7 beats. What is the heart rate, and what does it require?
choices: 42, begin compressions immediately
70, continue drying and stimulating only
70, begin positive-pressure ventilation
120, monitor and keep warm
emt-obgyn-peds-l05.why: Seven beats in 6 seconds times 10 is a rate of 70, which is under 100 and demands positive-pressure ventilation at 40 to 60 per minute. Compressions wait until 30 seconds of chest-rising ventilation has failed to bring the rate above 60.

emt-obgyn-peds-l05.q: A newborn is jittery, floppy and feeding poorly 40 minutes after birth. The mother has diabetes. What should you check?
choices: Blood glucose, because newborns of diabetic mothers drop their sugar
Blood pressure in all four limbs
Rectal temperature only, since cold explains all of it
Pupil size and reactivity
emt-obgyn-peds-l05.why: Infants of diabetic mothers burn through glucose quickly after the maternal supply stops, and jitteriness with poor feeding is the classic picture. Temperature matters too, but glucose is the check that changes treatment, and newborn blood pressures and pupils are not field-useful here.

emt-obgyn-peds-l06.q: A 9-year-old fell from a tree. His systolic pressure is 84 mmHg. Using the age formula, how do you read that number?
choices: Below the floor of 88, so he is in decompensated shock
Exactly at the floor of 84, so he is stable
Above the floor of 79, so it is acceptable for now
The formula does not apply over age 8
emt-obgyn-peds-l06.why: Seventy plus twice the age gives 70 plus 18, a floor of 88 mmHg, so 84 is below it and this child is decompensated. Any answer that calls 84 acceptable ignores that the formula applies through age 10.

emt-obgyn-peds-l06.q: A 5-month-old is limp, stares through you, and has a weak whimpering cry, but her breathing is unlabored and her skin is pink with brisk capillary refill. Which PAT pattern is this and what does it point to?
choices: Appearance abnormal only, pointing to a brain problem such as low glucose, a toxin or a seizure
Breathing abnormal only, pointing to early respiratory distress
Skin abnormal only, pointing to compensated shock
All three abnormal, pointing to cardiopulmonary failure
emt-obgyn-peds-l06.why: Only the appearance arm is abnormal, which points at the brain: hypoglycemia, a toxin, a postictal state or a head injury. Calling this respiratory or shock ignores the normal work of breathing and normal skin signs you just described.

emt-obgyn-peds-l07.q: A 3-year-old had a 2-minute generalized seizure with a temperature of 103 F. He is now awake, clingy and normal. The parents want to stay home. What is correct?
choices: He can stay home if the fever comes down with acetaminophen
He can stay home because febrile seizures are harmless
Transport, because every first febrile seizure needs evaluation
Transport only if the seizure lasted more than 5 minutes
emt-obgyn-peds-l07.why: A first febrile seizure gets evaluated even when the child looks perfect afterward, because the fever's source has not been identified. Most febrile seizures are indeed benign, but that is a conclusion the hospital reaches, not one you reach on the living-room floor.

emt-obgyn-peds-l07.q: You find a 2-month-old unresponsive and pulseless in a crib with no signs of irreversible death. What is your approach to the family?
choices: Ask who put the baby down and how long the baby was unattended
Begin resuscitation, disturb the scene as little as possible, and use plain, blameless language
Delay resuscitation until law enforcement has photographed the scene
Tell the family the baby is gone before you begin so they can say goodbye
emt-obgyn-peds-l07.why: Resuscitate unless there are obvious signs of irreversible death, preserve the scene, and speak without implying fault. Interrogating the family or delaying care for photographs is both harmful and outside your role.

emt-obgyn-peds-l08.q: An 88-year-old nursing home resident is confused and weak. Temperature 98.4 F, HR 104, BP 94/56, respirations 24. Which conclusion is correct?
choices: Infection is unlikely because she has no fever
Sepsis remains very likely, because older patients often cannot mount a fever
The findings fit dehydration only and she can be left with staff
The respiratory rate of 24 is normal for her age
emt-obgyn-peds-l08.why: A blunted fever response is the rule in the very old, so a normal temperature never rules out sepsis; confusion, a rising rate and a soft pressure do the arguing instead. A respiratory rate of 24 is abnormal at any adult age.

emt-obgyn-peds-l08.q: A family presents a valid DNR for a patient who is short of breath but still awake with a pulse. What does the DNR change?
choices: Nothing yet; oxygen, positioning, comfort and transport all continue
You must withhold oxygen because that is a resuscitative measure
You cannot transport a patient with a DNR
You may not assist ventilations under any circumstance
emt-obgyn-peds-l08.why: A DNR limits resuscitation at the moment of arrest; it never cancels comfort, oxygen, positioning or transport. Reading it as an order to withhold ordinary care is a common and serious error.

emt-obgyn-peds-l09.q: A 4-year-old with asthma can speak only single words, sits forward and refuses to lie down, with retractions and SpO2 of 89%. How do you grade this?
choices: Mild
Moderate
Severe
Respiratory failure
emt-obgyn-peds-l09.why: Single-word speech with SpO2 under 90% and deep retractions is a severe attack, which earns back-to-back treatments where protocol allows. Failure would add a quiet chest, drowsiness and poor effort, which this child does not yet show.

emt-obgyn-peds-l09.q: A metered-dose albuterol inhaler with a spacer is used on a 5-year-old. How much drug is in each puff, and how does it compare to a nebulizer for a moderate attack?
choices: 90 mcg per puff, and with a spacer it works about as well as a nebulizer
2.5 mg per puff, and it is always weaker than a nebulizer
90 mcg per puff, but it is useless without a nebulizer as well
180 mcg per puff, and a spacer is optional in children
emt-obgyn-peds-l09.why: An albuterol MDI delivers 90 mcg per puff and, used with a spacer, matches nebulized therapy for mild and moderate attacks. The 2.5 mg figure is the nebulizer dose, and a spacer is essential, not optional, in a child.

emt-obgyn-peds-l10.q: A parent says their 2-year-old swallowed a shiny coin-shaped battery an hour ago. The child is breathing normally and playing. What is the correct urgency?
choices: Nonurgent; advise a follow-up with the pediatrician tomorrow
Emergency transport now, because button batteries burn tissue within about 2 hours
Give the child water and watch for 4 hours at home
Transport only if the child develops stridor or drooling
emt-obgyn-peds-l10.why: A lodged button battery causes a current that burns through tissue in as little as 2 hours, so a well-appearing child still goes immediately. Waiting for symptoms means waiting for a perforation.

emt-obgyn-peds-l10.q: A 3-year-old had a coughing fit two weeks ago that everyone forgot about. He now has a lingering cough and a wheeze heard on the right side only. What should you suspect?
choices: Asthma presenting for the first time
Pneumonia in the right lower lobe
A retained foreign body in the right bronchus
Bronchiolitis
emt-obgyn-peds-l10.why: A one-sided wheeze after a witnessed choking episode is a retained foreign body, usually in the right bronchus because it is straighter. Asthma and bronchiolitis wheeze on both sides, and pneumonia would be expected to bring a fever and an ill appearance.

emt-obgyn-peds-l11.q: A 30 kg 10-year-old has a systolic pressure of 86 mmHg after a fall. Using the floor for his age, how do you read it?
choices: Acceptable, since 86 is above the 70 floor used in infants
Decompensated shock, because at 10 years the floor is 90 mmHg
Normal, since the formula stops applying at age 8
Compensated shock, because the pressure is still measurable
emt-obgyn-peds-l11.why: At 10 years and above the working floor is 90 mmHg, so 86 is decompensated shock and a near-arrest finding. A measurable pressure does not make it compensated, and the infant floor of 70 does not apply to him.

emt-obgyn-peds-l11.q: An ALS crew asks for a weight so they can dose a fluid bolus for a 15 kg toddler in shock. What volume should you expect, and over what time?
choices: 150 mL over an hour
300 mL over 5 to 20 minutes
600 mL as fast as possible
1,000 mL over 30 minutes
emt-obgyn-peds-l11.why: Twenty mL/kg times 15 kg is 300 mL, given over roughly 5 to 20 minutes and then reassessed. Ten mL/kg over an hour is too little and too slow, and 600 or 1,000 mL at once overshoots the first bolus badly.

emt-obgyn-peds-l12.q: A caregiver reports a forehead scanner reading of 99.2 F in a 4-week-old who has been feeding poorly. What is the right interpretation?
choices: The fever is ruled out and the infant can be watched at home
The route is unreliable at this age, so a reassuring reading does not clear the infant
A temporal reading runs high, so the true temperature is even lower
Only a tympanic reading would settle the question
emt-obgyn-peds-l12.why: Temporal and axillary readings run low and tympanic is unreliable under 6 months, so rectal is the standard under 3 months and a low forehead number proves nothing. Poor feeding in a 4-week-old is itself a red flag regardless of the number.

emt-obgyn-peds-l12.q: You are giving a radio report on a febrile 26-day-old. Which sentence is most useful to the receiving team?
choices: The baby looks sick and the parents are very worried
Twenty-six days old, rectal 101.2, two ounces since midnight instead of eight, one wet diaper since 8 p.m.
Febrile infant, vitals stable, ETA 10 minutes
Possible sepsis, request a pediatric bed
emt-obgyn-peds-l12.why: Age in days, the measured temperature with its route, feeding volume and wet diapers give the team the exact data that drives their workup. Adjectives like sick or stable and a bare label such as possible sepsis carry no information they can act on.

emt-obgyn-peds-l13.q: A 12-year-old is struck in the chest by a line drive and collapses. He is pulseless. What is the correct action?
choices: Immediate CPR and apply the AED
Check for rib fractures before moving him
Assume commotio cordis is untreatable and check for other injuries
Give 2 rescue breaths and wait 2 minutes before compressions
emt-obgyn-peds-l13.why: Commotio cordis throws a structurally normal heart into ventricular fibrillation, and early CPR plus defibrillation is the only thing that reverses it. Delaying to examine ribs or to breathe first wastes the minutes that decide survival.

emt-obgyn-peds-l13.q: A 6-year-old restrained in a lap belt only has a horizontal bruise across the lower abdomen after a highway crash. His vitals are normal and he says he feels fine. What does the bruise tell you?
choices: It is a superficial contusion and he can be released to the parents
It predicts hollow organ injury and a possible spine fracture behind it
It is only significant if the abdomen is already rigid
It suggests bleeding into the abdominal wall, not the abdomen
emt-obgyn-peds-l13.why: A seatbelt sign marks the force that tears bowel and fractures the lumbar spine behind it, and both declare themselves later, not now. Normal vitals in a child never rule out abdominal bleeding, because pressure falls last.

emt-obgyn-peds-l14.q: A child has a 4.0 tracheostomy tube that is plugged. What size suction catheter should you use, and where does that number come from?
choices: 4 Fr, matching the tube size
8 Fr, about twice the tube size
12 Fr, three times the tube size
16 Fr, the standard adult size
emt-obgyn-peds-l14.why: The catheter French size is roughly twice the tube size, so a 4.0 tube takes an 8 Fr catheter. A same-size catheter cannot clear the tube and an oversized one occludes it completely while you suction.

emt-obgyn-peds-l14.q: A tube-fed 8-year-old with a neurologic injury missed two feeds and is now acting differently. What should you check early?
choices: Blood glucose, since these children have almost no glucose reserve
Pupil size, since the shunt must be blocked
Temperature, since missed feeds cause fever
Nothing; missed feeds do not cause symptoms
emt-obgyn-peds-l14.why: Children who depend on tube feeds have very little stored glucose, so a missed feed plus a behavior change is hypoglycemia until the meter says otherwise. Not every device child has a shunt, and missed feeds do not produce fever.

emt-obgyn-peds-l15.q: After a field delivery you have placed four fully soaked perineal pads in 12 minutes. Roughly how much blood is that, and what does it mean?
choices: About 100 mL, within normal limits
About 400 mL, approaching the 500 mL hemorrhage threshold
About 1,000 mL, immediately fatal
The pads cannot be used to estimate blood loss
emt-obgyn-peds-l15.why: A fully soaked perineal pad holds roughly 100 mL, so four is about 400 mL and she is closing on the 500 mL definition of hemorrhage with the clock still running. Counting pads and reporting a time is exactly how blood loss is estimated in the field.

emt-obgyn-peds-l15.q: A patient in preterm labor at 33 weeks says her water broke 40 minutes ago. Which two details matter most in your report?
choices: Her pain score and her last meal
The time the membranes ruptured and the color of the fluid
Her blood type and her prenatal vitamin
The number of prior cesarean sections and her weight
emt-obgyn-peds-l15.why: Time of rupture starts the clock on infection risk, and fluid color flags meconium or blood, both of which change the delivery team's preparation. Pain score, diet and vitamins do not alter what the receiving hospital sets up.

emt-obgyn-peds-l16.q: You are running a newborn resuscitation with compressions. How many compressions and how many breaths does the baby receive in one full minute?
choices: 100 compressions and 10 breaths
90 compressions and 30 breaths
120 compressions and 12 breaths
60 compressions and 60 breaths
emt-obgyn-peds-l16.why: The 3-to-1 ratio at 120 events per minute works out to 90 compressions and 30 breaths each minute. The 100 to 120 compression figure and low breath counts come from adult CPR, which does not apply to a newborn.

emt-obgyn-peds-l16.q: A newborn's chest is not rising with bag-valve-mask ventilation. What is the correct order of fixes?
choices: Compressions, then epinephrine, then suction
Mask adjust, reposition, suction, open the mouth, increase pressure, alternative airway
Increase pressure first, then suction, then reposition
Suction deeply, then start compressions
emt-obgyn-peds-l16.why: MR SOPA runs in that order deliberately: the free mechanical fixes come before raising pressure or changing the airway. Adding compressions or drugs to ventilation that is not moving the chest accomplishes nothing.

emt-obgyn-peds-l17.q: An 80-year-old stands up and her BP falls from 132/78 to 108/70 within 2 minutes, with a pulse rise from 74 to 98. How do you read this?
choices: Normal, because the systolic stayed above 100
Orthostatic hypotension, since the systolic dropped 24 mmHg within 3 minutes
Not orthostatic, because the diastolic fell only 8 mmHg
Not interpretable without a third reading at 10 minutes
emt-obgyn-peds-l17.why: A drop of 20 mmHg systolic or 10 mmHg diastolic within 3 minutes of standing defines orthostatic hypotension, and 24 mmHg clears that bar on its own. Either criterion is enough, so the unchanged diastolic does not cancel it.

emt-obgyn-peds-l17.q: A 79-year-old on digoxin reports nausea and says lights have yellow-green halos around them. Her pulse is 48 and irregular. What does this pattern suggest?
choices: Digoxin toxicity
A new stroke affecting the visual cortex
Anticholinergic effect from her other medications
Acute angle-closure glaucoma
emt-obgyn-peds-l17.why: Nausea, yellow-green halos and a slow or irregular pulse is the classic digoxin toxicity triad, and it builds quietly as kidney function declines. A stroke would bring focal deficits, and anticholinergics cause confusion and retention rather than halos and bradycardia.

quiz.q: A 35-week pregnant patient is struck by a car. She is alert, BP 122/76, HR 112, and has a pelvic injury with obvious external bleeding. What best summarizes your priorities?
choices: High-flow oxygen, bleeding control, left tilt, warmth and rapid trauma-center transport
Assess fetal heart tones before treating the mother
Place her supine and flat to keep the spine aligned
Delay transport to obtain a full obstetric history
quiz.why: The best fetal care is a warm, oxygenated, well-perfused mother, so treat her injuries and tilt her left. Fetal heart tones change nothing an EMT can do, and flat supine positioning at 35 weeks compresses the vena cava and drops her pressure further.

quiz.q: Roughly how much blood can a third-trimester patient lose before her blood pressure finally falls?
choices: About 10% of her volume
About 15% of her volume
About 30 to 35% of her volume
About 50% of her volume
quiz.why: The extra 1 to 1.5 liters of pregnancy volume lets her hold pressure until roughly 30 to 35% is gone, by which point the fetus has been underperfused for a while. The 10 and 15% figures would be true of a non-pregnant patient, and 50% would be near arrest.

quiz.q: You are ventilating an unresponsive 32-week pregnant patient. Which technique detail matters most, and why?
choices: Use large volumes because her oxygen demand is higher
Ventilate gently to just visible chest rise, with suction ready, because aspiration risk is high
Hyperventilate to 30 breaths per minute to protect the fetus
Avoid an oropharyngeal airway in every pregnant patient
quiz.why: Delayed gastric emptying, a relaxed valve at the top of the stomach and high abdominal pressure make aspiration the main hazard, so use only enough volume to raise the chest and keep suction on. Large volumes force air into the stomach, and hyperventilation harms rather than helps.

quiz.q: A 32-week pregnant patient is bleeding heavily from the vagina. Your partner asks for the trauma dressings to pack the vagina and slow it down. What is your response?
choices: Never pack the vagina; place and count external pads and transport
Pack only if the bleeding soaks more than one pad per minute
Pack with sterile gauze and hold pressure during transport
Pack only after obtaining online medical direction
quiz.why: Nothing is ever placed in the vagina in the field, because packing can worsen a previa, hide the true loss and injure tissue. External pads, counted and timed, are how you estimate loss while oxygen, warmth and speed do the real work.

quiz.q: A woman delivered 9 days ago and now has a generalized seizure at home. Her BP is 172/108. Which statement is correct?
choices: Eclampsia is impossible after delivery, so this is a new seizure disorder
Eclampsia can occur up to 6 weeks postpartum and this fits it
This must be a stroke, since eclampsia ends with the placenta
Postpartum seizures are always caused by low blood sugar
quiz.why: Eclampsia can appear up to about 6 weeks after delivery, and a seizure with a pressure of 172/108 in that window is eclampsia until proven otherwise. Delivery lowers the risk but does not end it, and glucose should be checked without assuming it is the cause.

quiz.q: A 31-week pregnant patient fell down four stairs. She has constant abdominal pain, a firm tender uterus, and no vaginal bleeding at all. HR 118, BP 104/62. What is the greatest danger?
choices: Concealed bleeding behind a partially separated placenta
The absent bleeding rules out placental injury
A ruptured ectopic pregnancy
Supine hypotensive syndrome from lying on the stretcher
quiz.why: Abruption can bleed entirely behind the placenta, so no visible blood is reassuring only to someone who does not know that. An ectopic is a first-trimester event, and supine hypotension does not cause a rigid, tender uterus.

quiz.q: Which finding in a third-trimester bleeding patient points toward previa rather than abruption?
choices: A board-like uterus with dark bleeding
A soft, non-tender uterus with painless bright red bleeding
Recent blunt trauma to the abdomen
Severe constant pain with a rising heart rate
quiz.why: Previa is painless bright red bleeding from a placenta covering the cervix, and the uterus stays soft. A rigid tender uterus, dark blood, trauma and severe constant pain all belong to abruption.

quiz.q: You have just delivered the head of a term newborn. What is the single next thing you do before delivering the shoulders?
choices: Suction the mouth and then the nose routinely
Clamp the cord at 6 and 9 inches
Apply gentle downward traction on the head
Check the neck for a cord looped around it
quiz.why: The instant the head is out, run a finger around the neck to find a nuchal cord, because a tight one cuts off oxygen the moment the body delivers. Routine suctioning is no longer recommended, clamping comes after the birth, and traction on the head is never correct.

quiz.q: A newborn delivers vigorously at 39 weeks and is crying. When should the cord be clamped?
choices: After 1 to 3 minutes, so extra blood transfers from the placenta
Immediately, to prevent blood flowing back to the placenta
After the placenta delivers, whenever that happens
Only at the hospital, never in the field
quiz.why: A vigorous term newborn benefits from 1 to 3 minutes of delayed clamping, which moves extra blood from the placenta to the baby. Immediate clamping is reserved for a baby who needs resuscitation, and waiting for the placenta would delay both care and transport.

quiz.q: The placenta delivers 15 minutes after the baby. What do you do with it?
choices: Discard it in the biohazard bag on scene
Place it in a bag and transport it with the mother
Leave it attached to the newborn until arrival
Examine it and document whether it is complete
quiz.why: The placenta goes in a bag and travels with the patient so the hospital can check whether any fragment was retained, a cause of continued bleeding. Discarding it destroys that information, and judging completeness is not an EMT task.

quiz.q: A patient on her second pregnancy is 8 minutes from the hospital, contracting every 3 minutes for 70 seconds, and says she needs to have a bowel movement. You look and see the top of the head at the opening. What is correct?
choices: Drive fast; 8 minutes is short enough
Have her hold her legs together to delay delivery
Stop and prepare to deliver on scene
Place her knee-chest and transport emergently
quiz.why: Crowning plus the urge to push in a woman who has delivered before means the baby is coming now, so stop and deliver in a lit, roomy space. Holding her legs together can injure both patients, and knee-chest is for a prolapsed cord or limb presentation, not a normal delivery.

quiz.q: You have a hand inserted in the vagina holding the presenting part off a prolapsed cord. The patient is now at the emergency department doors. When do you remove your hand?
choices: As soon as you reach the hospital doors
During the transfer to the hospital bed
As soon as the cord stops pulsating
Only when an obstetrician takes over
quiz.why: Your hand keeps the baby's oxygen supply open, so it stays in place through the carry, the ride, the elevator and the transfer until an obstetrician assumes control. A cord that stops pulsating means the situation is worse, not finished.

quiz.q: Which finding makes field delivery impossible and mandates immediate transport for cesarean section?
choices: A single arm protruding from the vagina
A frank breech with the buttocks presenting
Meconium-stained amniotic fluid
Contractions 2 minutes apart in a first pregnancy
quiz.why: A limb presentation cannot deliver vaginally, so the answer is oxygen, knee-chest and emergent transport without pulling or pushing the limb. A breech can deliver in the field, meconium changes newborn care rather than the route, and frequent contractions alone are not a surgical indication.

quiz.q: A newborn delivers through thick green-brown fluid and is limp, apneic and blue. What is the correct action?
choices: Perform deep tracheal suctioning before any ventilation
Dry, warm, position and begin ventilation without deep suctioning
Suction the stomach to remove swallowed meconium
Begin chest compressions immediately
quiz.why: Current practice for a depressed meconium-stained newborn is to skip routine deep suctioning and get ventilation started, because time without breathing is the actual threat. Compressions come only after 30 seconds of chest-rising ventilation with a rate under 60.

quiz.q: At 1 minute a newborn has a pulse of 108, a strong cry, active motion, coughs when the bulb syringe touches the nose, and is blue at the hands and feet with a pink trunk. What is the APGAR?
quiz.why: Appearance scores 1 for acrocyanosis, and pulse, grimace, activity and respirations each score 2, totaling 9. A 10 would require complete pink coloring, which almost no newborn shows at 1 minute.

quiz.q: During newborn resuscitation the heart rate rises from 58 to 96 after a minute of compressions and ventilation. What changes?
choices: Stop both compressions and ventilation and monitor
Continue compressions until the rate is over 100
Stop compressions but continue ventilation
Stop ventilation and continue compressions alone
quiz.why: Compressions stop once the heart rate passes 60, but ventilation continues until the rate is over 100 with spontaneous breathing. Stopping ventilation is the error that sends the rate right back down, since newborn arrest is a breathing problem.

quiz.q: Why is warming and drying a newborn considered treatment rather than housekeeping?
choices: Because a wet towel interferes with the APGAR color score
Because drying prevents infection at the cord stump
Because heat loss lowers the newborn's heart rate directly through the skin
Because a cold newborn burns oxygen and glucose making heat, becomes acidotic and stops breathing well
quiz.why: Cold stress forces a newborn to spend oxygen and glucose generating heat, which drives acidosis and poor respiratory effort, so warming is resuscitation. Scoring and infection control are real concerns but neither explains why cold kills newborns.

quiz.q: A 7-month-old has an abnormal appearance, abnormal work of breathing and mottled skin. What does the PAT tell you?
choices: Cardiopulmonary failure requiring immediate airway support and transport
Respiratory distress, treatable with blow-by oxygen
Compensated shock with time to complete a full history
A primary brain problem such as a seizure or toxin
quiz.why: All three arms abnormal is cardiopulmonary failure, a child minutes from arrest who needs the airway opened and ventilation started now. A brain problem shows an abnormal appearance with normal breathing and skin, and compensated shock leaves appearance intact.

quiz.q: Which heart rate is most concerning in a 2-year-old with a head injury?
quiz.why: A rate of 52 in a toddler is bradycardia, which in children means hypoxia or rising intracranial pressure and demands immediate ventilation. The three higher rates are normal or expected for age and distress in a 2-year-old.

quiz.q: You are about to ventilate a 4-month-old. How should the head and shoulders be positioned?
choices: Head fully extended with a pad under the occiput
Head neutral with a small pad under the shoulders
Head turned to one side to drain secretions
Chin tucked toward the chest to open the airway
quiz.why: The large infant occiput flexes the neck when the child lies flat, so pad under the shoulders and keep the head neutral. Full extension kinks the soft trachea closed, and tucking the chin or turning the head makes the obstruction worse.

quiz.q: A 3-year-old with a fever is screaming and fighting the nonrebreather mask. His SpO2 reads 90% between screams. What is the best approach?
choices: Hold the mask on firmly until he accepts it
Withhold oxygen entirely since he is maintaining 90%
Use blow-by oxygen held by the caregiver and let him stay on her lap
Place a nasal cannula at 10 L/min
quiz.why: A calm child moves far more air than a fighting one, so blow-by on a caregiver's lap usually delivers more oxygen than a mask forced on a screaming face. Withholding oxygen at 90% is wrong, and 10 L/min through a pediatric cannula is uncomfortable and unnecessary.

quiz.q: A 5-year-old has a fever of 104 F and a purple rash on the abdomen that does not fade when you press a glass against it. What is your priority?
choices: Apply cool compresses to bring the fever down before moving
Delay transport until a parent arrives to sign consent
Treat it as a simple viral rash and transport non-emergently
Mask yourself and the patient, minimize contact, notify the hospital early and transport immediately
quiz.why: A non-blanching purple rash with fever is meningococcal disease until proven otherwise, which is both rapidly fatal and transmissible, so isolate, notify and move. Cooling measures and non-emergent transport waste the window, and consent is implied for an emergency in a minor.

quiz.q: Parents report their 2-month-old went limp and blue for about 20 seconds, then recovered completely. The infant now looks perfectly normal with normal vitals. What is correct?
choices: Transport every one of these events even when the infant looks normal
Advise the parents to follow up with the pediatrician this week
Obtain a refusal since the infant is asymptomatic
Transport only if the episode happened more than once
quiz.why: This describes a brief resolved unexplained event, and looking normal now does not exclude a serious underlying cause such as infection, seizure or a cardiac problem. Encouraging a refusal or a next-week follow-up on a 2-month-old is the wrong call regardless of how well the baby appears.

quiz.q: A caregiver says a 3-year-old drank an unknown amount of a cleaning product 20 minutes ago. What is the most useful thing you can do at the scene?
choices: Induce vomiting before the product is absorbed
Find out what, how much and when, and bring the container
Give milk to coat the stomach
Give activated charcoal from the jump bag
quiz.why: Identifying the substance, the amount and the time, and bringing the container, drives every decision the hospital and poison center make. Inducing vomiting risks a second caustic injury and aspiration, and milk and field charcoal are not indicated at the EMT level.

quiz.q: An 81-year-old fell and fractured a hip. Which detail in her medication list most changes how you think about her heart rate of 78?
choices: Atorvastatin
Levothyroxine
Metoprolol
Omeprazole
quiz.why: Metoprolol is a beta blocker, so it blunts the tachycardia that would otherwise signal blood loss, making a rate of 78 falsely reassuring. A statin, thyroid replacement and a stomach acid drug do not mask compensation for shock.

quiz.q: A 76-year-old man with a home ventilator is in distress, and the low-pressure alarm is sounding. What does that alarm most likely mean, and what do you do?
choices: An obstruction; suction the trach first
A dead battery; plug the unit in and wait
A high oxygen setting; turn the oxygen down
A leak or disconnection; disconnect the vent and bag him while you check the circuit
quiz.why: A low-pressure alarm points to a leak or a disconnected circuit, and the universal fix on any vent call is to take the machine out of the equation and bag through the trach. A high-pressure alarm is the one that means obstruction.

quiz.q: A 90-year-old with a central venous port needs oxygen and transport for weakness. Her daughter suggests you use the port for access. What is the correct action?
choices: Do not access the port; keep the site clean and tell the hospital it is there
Access it only if you flush it with saline first
Access it since it is faster than an intravenous line
Remove the port dressing to inspect the site for infection
quiz.why: Ports and central lines are not used or drawn from by EMTs; you keep the site clean and report its presence at the hospital. Flushing or accessing it risks infection and air embolism, and stripping the dressing serves no purpose in the field.

quiz.q: A 3-year-old with asthma is speaking in short phrases, sitting upright, with wheezing through all of exhalation and SpO2 of 92%. How do you grade the attack and what do you do?
choices: Mild; oxygen alone and transport
Moderate; oxygen to keep SpO2 at 94% or higher and albuterol per protocol
Severe; begin assisted ventilation immediately
Respiratory failure; prepare for CPR
quiz.why: Phrase-length speech with wheeze throughout exhalation and a saturation of 92% is a moderate attack, treated with oxygen and bronchodilator. Severe would mean single-word speech and SpO2 under 90%, and assisted ventilation belongs to a child who is tiring or quiet-chested.

quiz.q: You are bagging a 6-year-old in a severe asthma attack. After a minute his blood pressure falls from 104/62 to 78/50. What is the most likely cause?
choices: Sudden tension pneumothorax from the albuterol
An allergic reaction to the mask material
Breath stacking with air trapping, raising pressure in the chest
Overdose from the nebulized albuterol
quiz.why: Bagging a wheezing child too fast stacks breaths on top of trapped air, raising intrathoracic pressure until venous return and blood pressure drop. Slow down and allow full exhalation; a pneumothorax is possible but far less likely than the rate you control.

quiz.q: A 6-week-old with three days of congestion now wheezes and has two brief pauses in breathing during your assessment. He is feeding about half his usual amount. What is the key concern?
choices: He is too young for albuterol so nothing can be done
The wheeze means asthma and he needs an inhaler prescription
The pauses are normal periodic breathing and need no comment
Infants under 2 months with bronchiolitis can simply stop breathing, so he needs transport and close monitoring
quiz.why: Apnea is a recognized presentation of bronchiolitis in the youngest infants, and it can occur even when the lungs sound reasonable, so this baby is monitored the entire way in. Calling observed pauses normal or labeling a first wheeze at 6 weeks asthma both miss the danger.

quiz.q: A 2-year-old with croup has stridor at rest with visible retractions but is alert and interactive. How is this graded, and what is the field priority?
choices: Moderate; keep him calm on a caregiver, blow-by oxygen if needed, avoid procedures that make him cry
Mild; no treatment required
Severe; force a mask and begin assisted ventilation
Moderate; place an oral airway to bypass the swelling
quiz.why: Stridor at rest with retractions in an interactive child is moderate croup, and every intervention should avoid making him cry, because crying worsens the obstruction. An oral airway does nothing for swelling below the cords, and forcing a mask on an alert child makes him worse.

quiz.q: Why are chest compressions rather than back slaps used once a choking child becomes unresponsive?
choices: Because back slaps are only effective in patients who are standing
Because compressions generate higher airway pressure than back slaps
Because compressions restore circulation and the object no longer matters
Because the airway relaxes and the object falls out on its own
quiz.why: Compressions produce higher pressure in the airway than back slaps, which is what dislodges a wedged object in an unresponsive patient, and they buy circulation at the same time. The object still matters, which is why you look in the mouth before every rescue breath.

quiz.q: A 5-year-old has had a high fever for three days, holds his neck rigidly, refuses to turn his head, and has noisy breathing. He has no cough and no history of trauma. What should you suspect?
choices: Meningitis with neck stiffness
Croup
Retropharyngeal abscess
Foreign body aspiration
quiz.why: A young child with days of high fever who holds the neck rigid and refuses to move it fits a retropharyngeal abscess, an upper-airway infection. Croup barks and improves in cool air, aspiration starts in seconds with no preceding illness, and meningitis brings headache and photophobia rather than a refusal to move the neck to protect an airway.

quiz.q: A 10 kg 1-year-old has a scalp laceration that bled onto the floor. Your partner estimates 200 mL of loss and calls it minor. What fraction of the child's blood volume is that?
choices: About 5%
About 10%
About 25%
About 50%
quiz.why: At roughly 75 to 80 mL/kg a 10 kg child holds about 800 mL, so 200 mL is about a quarter of his supply, which is not minor. Adult intuitions about a small puddle are exactly what gets pediatric bleeding underestimated.

quiz.q: A 4-year-old with a fever of 103 F has warm flushed skin, a heart rate of 176, capillary refill of 3 seconds, and is difficult to rouse. Which type of shock is this?
choices: Hypovolemic shock from fever losses
Cardiogenic shock from myocarditis
Obstructive shock from tamponade
Distributive shock from sepsis
quiz.why: Fever with warm flushed skin, marked tachycardia and a change in mental status is distributive shock from sepsis, where the vessels dilate rather than the tank emptying. Hypovolemic and cardiogenic shock usually give cool, pale skin, and tamponade would add distended neck veins and muffled tones without the fever.

quiz.q: A 3-year-old in shock has a glucose reading of 48 mg/dL. Why does this matter?
choices: Low glucose travels with pediatric shock and needs correcting per protocol
It is normal for a child and needs no action
It confirms diabetes as the cause of the shock
It means the reading is faulty and should be ignored
quiz.why: Children have small glycogen stores and burn them fast in shock, so a value under 60 mg/dL needs correction alongside the shock care, varies by protocol. A single low reading in a sick child is not a diagnosis of diabetes and is not a reason to distrust the meter.

quiz.q: An unimmunized 7-week-old has a rectal temperature of 101.4 F. How does the missing vaccine history change your report?
choices: It does not matter, since infants that young have no vaccine protection anyway
It puts Haemophilus influenzae type b and pneumococcus back on the list and should be said out loud
It means the child must be transported to a pediatric specialty center only
It rules out a bacterial cause
quiz.why: An unimmunized infant loses the protection that removed Hib and pneumococcus from the routine list, and the receiving team needs that fact early. The first doses are given at 2 months, so a 7-week-old being unvaccinated is expected, but the caregiver's intent for future doses and any missed maternal care still belong in the report.

quiz.q: A father asks you to sponge his feverish 5-week-old with cool water and rubbing alcohol on the way in. What do you tell him?
choices: That is appropriate for temperatures above 102 F
Cool water is fine but alcohol is not
Neither; shivering raises the core temperature and alcohol can be absorbed through the skin
Only if the infant has already had acetaminophen
quiz.why: Cooling an infant by sponging triggers shivering, which raises core temperature and burns oxygen the baby cannot spare, and alcohol is absorbed through infant skin and is toxic. Neither method is appropriate at any temperature.

quiz.q: A 10-day-old has poor feeding, a brief seizure, and a cluster of small blisters on the scalp. What should this pattern raise?
choices: Chickenpox from a sibling
Diaper dermatitis spread to the scalp
A normal newborn rash called erythema toxicum
Herpes simplex acquired at delivery
quiz.why: Herpes simplex acquired at delivery classically appears at 5 to 14 days of life with poor feeding, seizures or grouped vesicles, and it is time-critical. Erythema toxicum is a benign blotchy rash without systemic signs, and neither chickenpox nor a diaper rash explains a seizure in a 10-day-old.

quiz.q: A 4-year-old restrained passenger in a rollover is apneic with a severe head injury. Your partner asks what ventilation rate to use and suggests bagging fast to blow off carbon dioxide. What is correct?
choices: Bag at 1 breath every 2 to 3 seconds; hyperventilation narrows brain vessels and worsens the injury
Bag at 1 breath per second to lower intracranial pressure
Bag at 1 breath every 5 seconds as in an adult
Bag only when the SpO2 drops below 90%
quiz.why: The goal is to prevent the second injury, which means normal ventilation at 1 breath every 2 to 3 seconds, an SpO2 of 94% or higher, adequate pressure and warmth. Hyperventilating drops carbon dioxide, constricts cerebral vessels and starves the injured brain.

quiz.q: A 6-year-old struck by a car has a scalp laceration, a GCS of 13, and a blood pressure of 76/44. What does the hypotension most likely mean?
choices: Blood loss inside the skull from the head injury
Bleeding somewhere other than the head, most likely the abdomen
A normal pressure for a 6-year-old after trauma
Spinal shock with no active bleeding
quiz.why: Only an infant with open sutures and a fontanelle can bleed enough inside the skull to cause shock, so in a 6-year-old hypotension means you have not found the bleeding yet. The floor for his age is 82 mmHg, so 76 is decompensated and demands a search of the abdomen, pelvis and femurs.

quiz.q: Which bruising pattern is most concerning under the TEN-4-FACES-P screen?
choices: A bruise on the shin of a 6-year-old who plays soccer
A bruise on the forehead of a 3-year-old who tripped
A bruise on the ear of a 2-year-old
A bruise on the knee of a 5-year-old
quiz.why: TEN-4 flags bruising of the torso, ear or neck in a child 4 or younger, and the ear is a location that ordinary play almost never reaches. Shins, knees and foreheads are the normal bruising sites of a mobile child.

quiz.q: A 5-year-old with chronic lung disease has a home baseline SpO2 of 88% and a baseline heart rate of 120. Today he is at 87% with a heart rate of 124 and his usual activity. What is the right interpretation?
choices: He is in respiratory failure and needs assisted ventilation
Give high-flow oxygen to bring him to 99%
Treat as compensated shock because the heart rate is above 120
He is essentially at his baseline, so evaluate the reason for the call instead of the numbers
quiz.why: The first question on any child with special healthcare needs is what is normal for him, and these numbers are his normal. Chasing a healthy child's targets here risks over-oxygenating him and distracts from whatever actually prompted the call.

quiz.q: A 7-year-old with a baclofen pump has a fever, rigid muscles and altered mental status. The family says the pump alarmed this morning. What does this represent?
choices: A true emergency from baclofen withdrawal requiring immediate transport
A routine pump alarm that can be addressed at the next clinic visit
Simple febrile illness unrelated to the pump
A shunt malfunction
quiz.why: Abrupt baclofen withdrawal from a failing pump causes fever, rigidity and altered mental status and can be fatal, so it is a load-and-go with the device information in hand. Treating it as a coincidental fever or deferring to clinic is the dangerous answer.

quiz.q: A parent of a technology-dependent child says she knows exactly what to do when this happens. What is the best use of that?
choices: Politely take over, since you are the trained provider
Ask her what she normally does and work with her
Ask her to wait outside so you can assess without distraction
Document her statement but follow only standard protocol
quiz.why: The caregiver has managed this airway or device hundreds of times and usually knows the fastest safe fix, so the first question on the call is what she normally does. Excluding her costs time and information without adding any safety.

quiz.q: A mother is bleeding after delivery, but her uterus is firm as a grapefruit and you can see steady bright bleeding from a perineal tear. Which of the four Ts is this, and what do you do?
choices: Tone; massage harder
Tissue; wait for the rest of the placenta
Trauma; apply direct pressure to the visible tear with gauze
Thrombin; warm her and transport without touching the tear
quiz.why: A firm uterus with visible bleeding points at trauma, and a perineal laceration gets direct external pressure. More massage on an already firm uterus accomplishes nothing, and warming matters but does not replace pressure on a bleeding tear.

quiz.q: You are preparing the ambulance for a likely preterm delivery. What temperature should the patient compartment be, and why?
choices: About 68 F, so the crew can work comfortably
About 90 F, to prevent any heat loss at all
Compartment temperature does not affect the newborn if blankets are used
About 78 F, because cold is the newborn's biggest enemy in the first minutes
quiz.why: Preheating to roughly 78 F or 26 C gives a wet newborn a fighting chance in the first 10 minutes, when heat loss drives acidosis and poor breathing. A comfortable crew temperature is far too cold for a newborn, and blankets alone cannot offset a cold room.

quiz.q: Which risk factor list best predicts postpartum hemorrhage from uterine atony?
choices: A long labor, a large baby, twins, many prior deliveries, or a very fast delivery
A first pregnancy, a short labor, and a small baby
Maternal age under 20 and a planned home birth
A history of cesarean section only
quiz.why: An overstretched or exhausted uterus is the one that fails to clamp down, which is why prolonged labor, macrosomia, twins, high parity and precipitous delivery head the list. A prior cesarean is the classic risk for uterine rupture, a different emergency.

quiz.q: A newborn is 1 minute old with a preductal SpO2 of 63%, a heart rate of 142 and a strong cry. What should you do?
choices: Apply a nonrebreather at 15 L/min
Keep her warm and monitor, because 60 to 65% is the target at 1 minute
Begin positive-pressure ventilation
Begin compressions since the saturation is under 70%
quiz.why: Preductal targets climb minute by minute, and 60 to 65% at 1 minute of life is exactly where a healthy newborn should be. Treating that number is how newborns get over-oxygenated, and the strong cry with a rate of 142 rules out any need for ventilation or compressions.

quiz.q: Which equipment list should be open and ready before a field delivery you expect to go badly?
choices: An adult bag-valve mask, a nasal cannula and a warm blanket
A pediatric nonrebreather, an oral airway and an AED
A 240 mL infant bag-valve mask with size 0 and 1 masks, two dry towels, a hat, a bulb syringe, two clamps and a clock
A nebulizer, a pulse oximeter and a cervical collar
quiz.why: The newborn setup is thermal gear, a correctly sized infant bag and masks, suction, clamps and a timer, because the algorithm runs on 30-second cycles. Adult bags deliver far too much volume, and an AED and collar have no role in newborn resuscitation.

quiz.q: In the first 5 seconds after a birth, which three questions decide whether the baby stays skin to skin or goes to the stretcher?
choices: Weight, length, and APGAR score
Heart rate, blood pressure, and temperature
Fluid color, cord length, and placental status
Term, good tone, breathing or crying
quiz.why: Term, good tone, and breathing or crying are the three rapid questions; three yes answers means dry the baby, place skin to skin and stop. APGAR is scored at 1 and 5 minutes and never delays care, and newborn blood pressure is not a field measurement.

quiz.q: A newborn is delivered at 30 weeks in the ambulance. Which thermal step is correct?
choices: Do not dry the body; wrap in plastic to the neck, dry the head only, and add a hat
Dry the body and head thoroughly, then wrap in two warm blankets
Apply heat packs directly against the skin
Leave the baby uncovered so you can watch color and chest rise
quiz.why: Under 32 weeks the evidence favors plastic wrap over the undried body with only the head dried and a hat added, targeting 36.5 to 37.5 C. Drying a very preterm baby removes the film that slows evaporation, and heat packs against skin cause burns.

quiz.q: An 86-year-old fell in the kitchen. She cannot say how she got to the floor and remembers nothing between standing at the sink and waking up there. How should you classify the event?
choices: A mechanical trip, since she was walking at the time
A syncopal event that must be worked up as cardiac or neurologic
Simple weakness from age, with no further workup needed
A seizure, since memory loss always means seizure
quiz.why: A gap in memory between standing and the floor means she lost consciousness, which makes this syncope and points at a cardiac or neurologic cause. A mechanical trip is something a patient can narrate, and memory loss alone does not establish a seizure.

quiz.q: Which handoff sentence about a confused 83-year-old is most useful to the emergency department?
choices: Patient is confused and has a history of dementia
Altered mental status, likely baseline
Daughter states patient normally does the crossword and cooks dinner; today she does not know her daughter's name
Patient is disoriented to time and place with a GCS of 14
quiz.why: A concrete baseline from two days ago is what separates delirium from dementia, and delirium is a medical emergency with a findable cause. Labels like confused or likely baseline and a bare GCS give the team no way to judge whether anything has changed.

quiz.q: An 87-year-old is quiet during your assessment, and her son answers every question directed at her and refuses to leave the room. She has bruising on both inner arms in different stages of healing. What is the best action?
choices: Confront the son about the bruising before transport
Say nothing, since the bruising has an innocent explanation in older skin
Refuse to transport until law enforcement arrives
Document the behavior and bruising factually, try for 60 seconds alone during the move, and report to Adult Protective Services
quiz.why: The behavioral pattern matters more than any single bruise, and the move to the stretcher is the natural chance to speak with her alone. You document facts and direct quotes and report to Adult Protective Services or, for a facility resident, the Ombudsman for the Institutionalized Elderly; confronting a caregiver can escalate the danger to the patient.
